title_en: Notice of the Supreme People's Court on Issuing the Summary of the National Symposium on Commutation of Sentence and Parole Work
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court

Circular on Issuing the Summary of the National Forum on Commutation and Parole Work

Fa (Ban) Fa [1989] No. 3

To all local people's courts at various levels, all military courts, all railway transport intermediate courts and basic level courts, and all maritime courts:

The Summary of the National Forum on Commutation and Parole Work is hereby issued to you for your careful study and implementation.

February 14, 1989

Summary of the National Forum on Commutation and Parole Work

The National Forum on Commutation and Parole Work was held in Beijing from November 25 to 29, 1988. Participants in this forum included directors or deputy directors of trial divisions responsible for commutation and parole work from higher people's courts of various provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government, and the Military Court of the People's Liberation Army; and presidents or division chiefs from some intermediate and basic level people's courts. Representatives from the Prison Procuratorial Department of the Supreme People's Procuratorate, the Bureau of Reform-through-Labor of the Ministry of Justice, and the Pre-trial Bureau of the Ministry of Public Security were invited to attend. The forum reviewed the situation of commutation and parole work in previous years, summarized and exchanged work experience, and studied issues such as how to correctly implement laws and policies, and how to perfect case-handling procedures and systems. The summary is as follows:

I

The forum was of the view that in recent years, people's courts at all levels across the country, in close cooperation with public security, procuratorial, and judicial administrative organs at all levels, have tried a large number of commutation and parole cases in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Criminal Law and the Criminal Procedure Law. From 1985 to the first half of 1988, a total of over 500,000 criminals received commutation or parole, and the work has been fruitful. Many courts also entered reform-through-labor institutions and, in conjunction with the pronouncement of commutation or parole rulings, conducted legal education for criminals. Through commutation and parole, obvious results have been achieved in motivating criminals to reform, stabilizing prison supervision order, and promoting comprehensive management of public security. The main problems currently existing in commutation and parole work are: the quality of case handling in a small number of cases is not high; some courts are not strict enough in implementing case-handling procedures and systems. These problems need to be seriously addressed.

II

The forum was of the view that the trial of commutation and parole cases must strictly adhere to national laws and policies. Based on relevant provisions and trial practice, the forum put forward the following opinions on how to specifically implement laws and policies:

(1) Conditions for Commutation and Parole

1. Conditions for Commutation

Criminals sentenced to public surveillance, criminal detention, fixed-term imprisonment, or life imprisonment may, if they truly demonstrate repentance or meritorious performance during the execution of their sentences, be granted commutation. Criminals sentenced to criminal detention or fixed-term imprisonment of not more than three years and placed on probation may, if they demonstrate outstanding repentance or meritorious performance during the probation period, have their original sentences reduced, with a corresponding reduction in the probation period.

"True repentance" mainly refers to the criminal's acceptance of the judgment and submission to the law; consistent compliance with prison discipline; active participation in political, cultural, and technical studies; and active participation in labor, protection of public property, and completion of labor tasks. If all four aspects are simultaneously present, it should be considered as true repentance. For criminals who file appeals during the execution of their sentences, specific circumstances should be analyzed case by case, and it should not be generally assumed that they do not accept the judgment or submit to the law.

"Meritorious performance" refers to: exposing or reporting criminal activities of criminals inside or outside the prison, which is verified to be true; stopping other criminals' escape, assault, destruction, or other criminal activities; making inventions, creations, or major technical innovations in production; sacrificing oneself to save others in daily production or life; making outstanding contributions in emergency rescue and disaster relief; or other outstanding deeds beneficial to the state and the people. If any of the above performances is present, it should be considered as meritorious.

2. Conditions for Parole

Criminals sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment who have served more than half of the original sentence, and criminals sentenced to life imprisonment who have actually served more than ten years, may be granted parole if they truly demonstrate repentance and are not likely to endanger society again. If there are special circumstances, the above requirements regarding the portion of sentence served may be waived.

"Not likely to endanger society again" means that the criminal has truly repented, has consistently performed well during the period of reform through labor, and is not likely to commit new crimes; or is an elderly, weak, sick, or disabled person who has lost the ability to commit crimes. "Special circumstances" generally refers to: the original work unit requests release on parole due to special needs in production or major scientific research; or other special circumstances.

(2) Commutation for Criminals Sentenced to Death with a Reprieve

Commutation for criminals sentenced to death with a reprieve is different from the commutation provided for in Article 71 of the Criminal Law. According to Article 46 of the Criminal Law, if a criminal sentenced to death with a reprieve truly demonstrates repentance during the execution period, after the two-year period expires, the sentence shall be commuted to life imprisonment; if the criminal truly demonstrates repentance and has meritorious performance, after the two-year period expires, the sentence shall be commuted to fixed-term imprisonment of not less than fifteen years and not more than twenty years. The above provisions must be strictly implemented. Based on legislative intent and trial practice experience, if a criminal sentenced to death with a reprieve does not have any aggravated circumstances of resisting reform during the execution period, after the two-year period expires, the sentence shall also be commuted to life imprisonment.

(3) Scope of Commutation

For criminals sentenced to life imprisonment, if they truly demonstrate repentance or meritorious performance during the execution period, after serving two years of imprisonment, commutation should be granted promptly. In order to align the commutation for life imprisonment criminals with the commutation for criminals sentenced to death with a reprieve and those sentenced to long-term fixed-term imprisonment, for those who truly demonstrate repentance, the sentence may generally be commuted to fixed-term imprisonment of not less than eighteen years and not more than twenty years; for those who truly demonstrate repentance and have meritorious performances, the sentence may be commuted to fixed-term imprisonment of not less than thirteen years and not more than eighteen years.

For criminals sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment, if they truly demonstrate repentance or meritorious performance during the execution period, the sentence may generally be reduced by not more than one year in a single commutation; if they truly demonstrate repentance and have meritorious performance, the sentence may generally be reduced by not more than two years in a single commutation; if they have major meritorious performance, the above limitations on the scope of commutation may be disregarded.

For criminals sentenced to public surveillance, criminal detention, or criminal detention or fixed-term imprisonment of not more than three years and placed on probation, if they truly demonstrate repentance or meritorious performance, appropriate commutation may be granted.

For the actual sentence served after one or more commutations, for those sentenced to public surveillance, criminal detention, or fixed-term imprisonment, the actual sentence served shall not be less than half of the original sentence; for those sentenced to life imprisonment, the actual sentence served shall not be less than ten years; for those sentenced to criminal detention on probation, the probation period shall not be less than one month; for those sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment on probation, the probation period shall not be less than one year.

Where the original sentence includes deprivation of political rights as a supplementary punishment, different treatments shall be applied based on different circumstances during commutation. Where the sentence is commuted from death with a reprieve to life imprisonment, the supplementary punishment of deprivation of political rights for life remains unchanged; where the sentence is commuted from death with a reprieve or life imprisonment to fixed-term imprisonment, the period of deprivation of political rights as a supplementary punishment shall be changed to not less than three years and not more than ten years; when a fixed-term imprisonment sentence is commuted, the supplementary punishment of deprivation of political rights may be appropriately reduced or not reduced; when a public surveillance sentence is commuted, the supplementary punishment of deprivation of political rights shall be dealt with according to the provisions of Article 51, paragraph 2 of the Criminal Law.

(4) Starting Point and Interval for Commutation of Fixed-term Imprisonment Criminals

For criminals sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of five years or more, commutation may generally be granted only after serving at least one and a half years of the sentence; the interval between two commutations should generally be at least one year. For criminals sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of less than five years, the above time limits may be appropriately shortened by analogy. For those with meritorious performance, the above time limits may be disregarded.

(5) Commutation and Parole for Certain Types of Criminals

The trial of commutation and parole cases is primarily based on the criminal's reform performance, but the circumstances of the original sentence should also be considered. For serious counter-revolutionary elements, ringleaders and principal offenders of criminal groups, recidivists, and habitual offenders, commutation and parole shall be handled with special caution and strict control.

III

The forum was of the view that the jurisdiction and trial procedures for commutation and parole cases need to be further clarified and strictly implemented. The forum put forward the following opinions:

(1) Jurisdiction over Commutation and Parole Cases

For several years, the Supreme People's Court and relevant departments have jointly issued some documents, clearly stipulating the jurisdiction over commutation and parole cases, namely: commutation for criminals sentenced to death with a reprieve and commutation and parole for criminals sentenced to life imprisonment shall be under the jurisdiction of the higher people's court of the place of imprisonment; commutation and parole for criminals sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment (including criminals originally sentenced to death with a reprieve or life imprisonment whose sentences have been commuted to fixed-term imprisonment), and commutation for criminals sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of not more than three years and placed on probation, shall be under the jurisdiction of the intermediate people's court of the place of imprisonment; commutation for criminals sentenced to criminal detention (including those sentenced to criminal detention and placed on probation) and public surveillance shall be under the jurisdiction of the local basic level people's court; commutation and parole for criminals serving sentences in detention houses (criminals sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of not more than one year and those whose remaining sentence after deduction of pre-sentence detention is less than one year, as well as individual criminals with a remaining sentence of more than one year who are approved by relevant departments due to special needs) shall be under the jurisdiction of the local people's court at the same level. These provisions shall still be seriously implemented.

(2) Procedures and Systems for Trying Commutation and Parole Cases

1. When filing a case, the court shall examine whether the materials and procedures submitted by the executing organ are complete and sufficient. The submitted materials include: the petition for commutation or parole, the criminal's assessment and evaluation form, the approval form for rewards and punishments, copies of the final judgment and ruling of the court of last instance, copies of previous commutation rulings, and evidentiary materials on the specific facts of the criminal's repentance or meritorious performance. Where it is found upon examination that the materials are incomplete or the procedures are insufficient, the executing organ shall be notified to supplement the materials or return the case for supplementary investigation.

2. When trying commutation and parole cases, the specific facts of the criminal's true repentance or meritorious performance shall be carefully examined. Some cases shall be selected as focal points for verification by entering the reform-through-labor institution to understand the criminal's reform situation during the execution period.

3. Commutation and parole cases shall be tried by a collegial panel.

4. The commutation or parole ruling shall briefly state the facts of the criminal's true repentance or meritorious performance, and cite the relevant articles of the Criminal Law and the Criminal Procedure Law. For cases where commutation is granted, the starting and ending dates of the sentence shall be indicated; for cases where parole is granted, the starting and ending dates of the parole supervision period shall be indicated.

5. The commutation or parole ruling shall be examined and signed by the division chief or the responsible president of the court.

6. The commutation or parole ruling may be pronounced directly by the people's court or may be entrusted to the executing organ for pronouncement. The people's court shall simultaneously serve a copy of the ruling to the court that rendered the original judgment and the people's procuratorate responsible for supervising the reform-through-labor institution.

7. Where the president of the court or a higher people's court discovers that a commutation or parole ruling is indeed erroneous, or where a people's procuratorate files a protest, the matter shall be handled through the trial supervision procedure.

IV

The forum was of the view that to further improve commutation and parole work, it is necessary to enhance the understanding of commutation and parole work. Trying commutation and parole cases is part of the judicial power granted to people's courts by law and is a routine task in the criminal trial work of people's courts. Doing a good job in commutation and parole work is of great significance for strengthening the socialist legal system, maintaining the seriousness of the law and the judgments of people's courts, promoting the reform of criminals, and strengthening comprehensive management of public security. People's courts at all levels shall strictly follow the relevant provisions of the Criminal Law and the Criminal Procedure Law, adhere to the principle of taking facts as the basis and law as the criterion, and actively and carefully try every commutation and parole case to ensure the quality of case handling.

People's courts at all levels shall regard commutation and parole work as an important task in criminal trial work and place it on their agenda. The responsible president shall frequently supervise and inspect, study and solve problems and practical difficulties in the work, and personally attend to some major and difficult cases. Higher courts shall strengthen investigation and research, grasp the work situation, summarize and promote good experiences, promptly help lower courts study problems in their work, and exercise supervisory and guiding roles.

People's courts at all levels shall make overall plans, appropriately adjust and strengthen the case-handling force for commutation and parole work. Higher and intermediate people's courts, due to the large number of cases and heavy workload, shall be staffed with cadres commensurate with the tasks; basic level people's courts shall have dedicated personnel and maintain stability.

People's courts shall strengthen close cooperation with reform-through-labor departments and other relevant departments, regularly exchange information and views; for commutation and parole cases submitted by executing organs, people's courts shall promptly try them and issue rulings; in conjunction with the reward and punishment activities of executing organs, when pronouncing rulings, people's courts shall conduct legal education and propaganda for criminals to expand the effect of case handling.
